asks: How is a report matched to a fact, and a process to a run?
answer: A report is matched to a fact by exact keys, never by nearness in time. Where a report falls is read from its source's own numbers, not from a clock: at each checkpoint the probe is told of it and writes a line that marks it in its count, so a report numbered before the mark falls before the checkpoint even when it arrives after. A report that no mark places is not compared, and stays unverified. A file report matches a file fact when the computer and the path are the same and the report falls between the two checkpoints the fact covers. File facts have the grain of checkpoints (`file-changes-from-outside`), so a file report with no fact is not contradicted, since a write can be undone or repeat the same bytes before the next checkpoint: it stays unverified. A report of a connection that leaves the computer matches a connection fact when the computer, the local port, the host and the port are the same and the boundary saw that connection between the two marks the report falls between; when the boundary saw more than one such connection there, the report is not compared and stays unverified, and when it saw none, the report gets a mismatch, since every such connection crosses the boundary. A process belongs to a run when a walk up its parents, or its group where the system has one, reaches the launch of an agent program; when the two reach different launches, it belongs to no run, and both runs are named. A process whose chain is broken, by a gap or a missing parent, belongs to no run, and what it wrote is unattributed. A fact with no report stays unattributed. When several runs report writing the same path between the same two checkpoints, the change is not shared out: it is unattributed, and the runs that reported it are named. Tests with reports made up by a hostile program check each case. To find out: how the mark is placed, and how a write the computer had not yet saved to its disk at the checkpoint is placed.
